scanner.hint: Select a layer, then tap any glowing region of the body to open its detail panel.

regions.carlitosNote: In microgravity, body fluids drift toward the head. That mild pressure rise is why headaches are more common up here — I track them so the medical team sees the pattern early.
regions.name: Brain & head
regions.summary: Mild intracranial pressure increase from the upward fluid shift.

regions.carlitosNote: Without gravity pulling fluids down, the eye changes shape very slightly. It is called SANS and crews have monitored it for years — your checks are right on schedule.
regions.name: Eyes & vision
regions.summary: Slight flattening at the back of the eye — the known SANS pattern.

regions.carlitosNote: Your heart is a muscle, and in space it does not have to pump against gravity — so it can slowly detrain. Your cardio sessions are keeping it in shape. Well done.
regions.name: Heart
regions.summary: Cardiac muscle mass, rhythm and blood pressure all stable.

regions.carlitosNote: A small, steady mass loss is expected on long missions — your nutrition and exercise plans are designed around it. Nothing here needs action.
regions.name: Abdomen & core
regions.summary: Digestion, hydration and fluid balance nominal.

regions.carlitosNote: Funny side effect of space: without gravity squeezing your spine, you literally grow a few centimeters by 'morning'. Your discs re-hydrate — the stiffness usually fades after a good exercise session.
regions.name: Lumbar spine
regions.summary: Vertebral discs expand slightly without gravity — mild stiffness reported.
regions.trend: Transient height gain of about 4 cm

regions.carlitosNote: Your femur is the longest, strongest bone you have — and in microgravity it slowly gives up calcium because it is not carrying your weight. The good news: your loss rate is slowing and it stays inside mission limits. Keep up the resistance training and we will watch it together.
regions.name: Femur (left)
regions.summary: Load-bearing bone losing density slowly under reduced gravity — countermeasures are limiting the loss.

regions.carlitosNote: Muscles on the front of the thighs do a lot of quiet work on Earth — standing, walking, braking. In orbit they get lazy. Daily resistance exercise is the antidote, and your numbers show it is working, just not completely yet.
regions.name: Quadriceps (right)
regions.summary: Front-thigh muscles thinning without daily gravity loading.

regions.carlitosNote: Your calves are the success story of this mission — the exercise prescription is tuned just right for them. If only the quadriceps took notes.
regions.name: Calves
regions.summary: Lower-leg muscles responding well to the resistance exercise plan.

carlitos.disclaimer: Carlitos explains and guides — he never diagnoses or prescribes. For medical decisions, talk to your flight surgeon.

messages.author: carlitos
messages.text: Welcome back, Commander. Systems are green and today's full-body scan finished two hours ago.

messages.author: carlitos
messages.text: Want to look at something specific? Try asking me: "I want to check my femur."

messages.author: user
messages.text: Carlitos, I want to check my femur.

messages.author: carlitos
messages.text: Easy. Switch to the Skeletal layer, then tap your left thigh — the femur panel opens with all your density readings. Short version: 1.18 g/cm², about 1.2% below pre-flight. That is normal for day 148, and your countermeasure exercise is holding the line.

protocols.kit: Radiation kit · service module, rack B2
steps: Move to the storm shelter in the service module immediately — do not stop to collect equipment.
Log your shelter entry time; flight control models your dose from it later.
Take the Radiation kit from rack B2: two anti-nausea doses and a dosimeter badge.
Stay inside until the station-wide all-clear, or 40 minutes minimum.
Report any headache, nausea or unusual metallic taste in the symptom log when you return.
protocols.title: Solar particle event — shelter protocol

steps: Sit facing the A4 vision chart at arm's length — one eye covered, good light.
Read down the chart; note the lowest line you can resolve for each eye.
Compare with your last logged acuity: 20/25 on day 141.
If blur is sudden, one-sided or with flashes, log it as urgent — do not delay.
Record both readings in the symptom log; the flight surgeon trends SANS weekly.
protocols.title: Acute eye / SANS check

protocols.kit: Medical kit A · crew health station
steps: Stabilize the crew member: airway, bleeding, consciousness — in that order.
Open Medical kit A at the crew health station; the red tray holds the airway kit.
Take vitals every 15 minutes and write each reading on the triage card.
Keep the burst-report checklist running — it snapshots your vitals automatically.
Retry the comms link every 15 minutes; until it opens, continue the protocol.
protocols.title: Medical emergency onboard
